extracted.intended_audience: readers of biography and history of science; historians and students interested in Charles Darwin's life and scientific practice
extracted.subtask_description: Implicit guidance on the habits, ethics, and working practices of a scientific author (as exemplified by Charles Darwin): concision, citation practice, responses to criticism, judgement of sources, perseverance under ill-health, and professional generosity. Useful for thinking about good professional conduct in science and authorship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conciseness / aversion to lengthiness
rubrics_metrics.description: He had a horror of being lengthy, and seems to have been really much annoyed and distressed when he found how the 'Variations of Animals and Plants' was growing under his hands.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefers brevity; agrees with 'Tristram Shandy's' words: 'Let no man say, "Come, I'll write a duodecimo."' (anti-pattern: producing overly long, sprawling works that distress the author and reader).

rubrics_metrics.name: Respectful tone toward other authors
rubrics_metrics.description: His consideration for other authors was as marked a characteristic as his tone towards his reader. He speaks of all other authors as persons deserving of respect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even when thinking lightly of an author's work (e.g., experiments on Drosera) he framed his remarks so no one would suspect it; when encountering confused writings he often treated the fault as his own for not appreciating them. Express opinions on quoted works pleasantly and acknowledge private obligations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Generous praise combined with careful scrutiny
rubrics_metrics.description: It was delightful to draw for him, as he was enthusiastic in his praise of very moderate performances... Though he praised so generously, he always looked closely at the drawing, and easily detected mistakes or carelessness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage and praise collaborators and contributors but also inspect work closely for errors; combine warmth with critical attention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judgement of trustworthiness of sources/authors
rubrics_metrics.description: He had the keenest of instincts as to whether a man was trustworthy or not. He seemed to form a very definite opinion as to the accuracy of the men whose books he read; and made use of this judgment in his choice of facts for use in argument or as illustrations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess authors' reliability and accuracy before using their facts as evidence; practical selection of facts for argument should be informed by such judgement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strictness in quotation and literary honour
rubrics_metrics.description: He had a keen feeling of the sense of honour that ought to reign among authors, and had a horror of any kind of laxness in quoting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be meticulous in attribution and citation; avoid lax or careless quotation practices. This is part of a broader ethic that values truth over personal glory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dislike of seeking priority and contempt for love of fame
rubrics_metrics.description: He had a contempt for the love of honour and glory... Connected with his contempt for the undue love of fame, was an equally strong dislike of all questions of priority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid making priority disputes a central concern; focus on contributions to knowledge rather than personal fame. The correspondence around the 'Origin' illustrates his discomfort with priority quarrels (e.g., Wallace).

rubrics_metrics.name: Refraining from public reclamations and disputes
rubrics_metrics.description: His feeling about reclamations, including answers to attacks and all kinds of discussions, was strong... 'I was very sorry about your reclamation, as I think it is in every case a mistake and should be left to others.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid entering into public paper-warfare or heated replies to critics except rarely; motive includes delicate temperament and desire to avoid wasting time, energy, and temper. Note occasional lapses and later regret when one does reply.

rubrics_metrics.name: Openness to ideas from diverse people
rubrics_metrics.description: His respectful feeling was not only morally beautiful, but was I think of practical use in making him ready to consider the ideas and observations of all manner of people.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain an openness to observations and ideas from a wide range of contributors, even non-experts; but be ready to calibrate trustworthiness (see judgment criterion). He admitted he initially sometimes rated everything too highly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Persistent work and patience under ill-health
rubrics_metrics.description: If the character of my father's working life is to be understood, the conditions of ill-health, under which he worked, must be constantly borne in mind... he bore his illness with such uncomplaining patience ... for nearly forty years he never knew one day of the health of ordinary men.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sustained intellectual work can and often does occur under prolonged personal hardship; recognise constraints that ill-health places on productivity and the importance of support (e.g., spouse shielding from avoidable annoyances).

rubrics_metrics.name: Enthusiasm for hands-on observation and fieldwork
rubrics_metrics.description: He entomologized most industriously, picking up creatures as he walked along, and bagging everything which seemed worthy of being pursued, or of further examination... he armed me with a bottle of alcohol, in which I had to drop any beetle which struck me as not of a common kind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Active collection, close observation, and practical engagement with specimens are core habits of natural-history inquiry; mentoring others in these practices spreads scientific interest and skill.

rubrics_metrics.name: Generosity and warmth in collegial relations
rubrics_metrics.description: He was the most genial, warm-hearted, generous, and affectionate of friends; that his sympathies were with all that was good and true; and that he had a cordial hatred for everything false, or vile, or cruel, or mean, or dishonourable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cultivate geniality and generosity to foster durable friendships and collaborations; social conviviality (clubs, musical and dining gatherings) contributed to intellectual life and networks.
